absolute monarch: A king who has all the power by himself: he makes the laws, delivers justice and commands the army, without answering to anyone.
privilege: An advantage kept for some people only. Before 1789, nobles and clergy paid very few taxes: that was a privilege.
national assembly: The assembly of deputies elected by citizens to represent the nation. It votes the laws. It was born in 1789.
monarchy: A system in which a country is ruled by a king or queen, who often passes power on to their children.
republic: A system without a king, where power belongs to the people, who choose their representatives in elections. The word comes from the Latin res publica, "the public thing".
coup d'état: Taking power by force or by trickery, without respecting the law.
empire: A system ruled by an emperor. It also means a group of territories ruled by one country.
restoration: The return of kings to power in France, from 1814–1815 to 1830, after Napoleon's fall.
barricade: An obstacle built across a street with paving stones, furniture or carts, to protect people and block soldiers during a revolt.
july monarchy: The reign of King Louis-Philippe, from 1830 to 1848, born from the July Revolution of 1830.
colonisation: When a country takes control of a faraway territory and its people, often by force, to exploit and rule it.
abdicate: When a king or emperor gives up power and leaves the throne.
universal suffrage: The right to vote for all adult citizens. In 1848 it only included men; it became truly universal in 1944, when women got the vote.
slavery: The situation of a person who belongs to someone else, like an object. An enslaved person can be sold and is forced to work without pay.
decree: A written decision taken by the government that has the force of law.
crime against humanity: A very serious crime committed against whole populations, such as slavery or genocide. It can never be excused or forgotten by the law.
armistice: An agreement to stop the fighting during a war.
monarchist: A person who wants a king to rule the country.
paris commune: The revolutionary government elected by the people of Paris from March to May 1871, crushed by the army of the Versailles government.
deport: To send someone away by force, as a punishment, to a very distant place or to a camp.
amendment: A change proposed to a bill while deputies or senators are discussing it.
constitutional laws: The laws of 1875 that organised how the Third Republic worked: the president, the Chamber of Deputies and the Senate.
national anthem: A country's official song, played at ceremonies and sports matches. France's is La Marseillaise.
national holiday: The day a country celebrates its history. In France, it is 14 July.
motto: A short sentence that sums up an ideal. The Republic's motto is "Liberty, Equality, Fraternity".
freedom of assembly: The right to gather with other people to discuss or defend ideas, without asking for permission.
freedom of the press: The right to create newspapers and write what you think in them, including criticising the government, while respecting the law.
defamation: Saying or writing a false accusation in public that damages someone's reputation. It is against the law.
trade union: An association of workers who join together to defend their rights and working conditions.
centenary: The hundredth anniversary of an event.
free: Not costing anything. Since 1881, state school in France has been free.
compulsory: Something you must do. Since 1882, education has been compulsory for all children in France.
secular: Neutral about religion. A secular state school teaches no religion and respects all beliefs.
teacher: The person who teaches a class. In Jules Ferry's time, primary school teachers were called "instituteurs".
teacher training college: The school where future primary school teachers were trained, one in each département.
black hussars: The nickname Charles Péguy gave to the teachers of the Third Republic, dressed in black, who spread republican ideas.
inkwell: A small pot of ink set into a hole in the desk, into which you dipped your pen to write.
primary school certificate: The exam taken at about 12 at the end of primary school, from 1866 to 1989. It was called the "certif".
antisemitism: Hatred, contempt or prejudice against Jewish people. It is a form of racism and is punished by law.
freedom of expression: The right to say, write and publish what you think, while respecting the law and other people.
freedom of conscience: The right to believe or not to believe in a religion, and to change your religion.
secularism: In France, called laïcité: the principle that the state favours no religion. Everyone is free to believe or not, and the state stays neutral.
strike: When workers stop working together to demand better pay or better working conditions.
paid holidays: Days off during which employees are still paid. They have existed in France since 1936.
social rights: Rights linked to work and everyday life: the right to rest, to health care, to fair pay, to protection in hard times.
censorship: When those in power ban or remove articles, books or films that bother them.
dictatorship: A system in which one person or a small group has all the power, with no free elections and no respect for freedoms.
resistance: During the Second World War, all the people who fought against the German occupation and the Vichy regime.
suffragette: A woman who campaigned for women's right to vote.
ordinance: A decision taken by the government that has the same force as a law.
referendum: A vote in which all citizens are asked directly to answer "yes" or "no" to a question.
preamble: The text at the start of the Constitution that sets out the great principles and rights.
social security: The system created in France in 1945 that pays for health care, pensions and help for families, thanks to everyone's contributions.
constitution: A country's most important text. It sets the rules for how the powers work and the rights of citizens.
direct universal suffrage: When all voters vote themselves to choose a person, without going through intermediaries.
polling station: The room, often in a school or town hall, where voters go to vote on election day.
voting booth: The small booth with a curtain where a voter chooses their ballot in secret.
equality: Having the same rights and being treated in the same way as others.
co-education: Girls and boys learning together, for example in the same class.
adult: In law, a person who has reached the age of majority, 18 in France: they have all their rights as a citizen and are responsible for their actions.
death penalty: The punishment of executing a person convicted of a crime. It has been abolished in France since 1981.
convention on the rights of the child: The text adopted by the United Nations in 1989 that sets out the rights of all the world's children.
parity: Having as many women as men, for example among candidates or elected officials.
citizen: A person who belongs to a country, with rights (like voting) and duties (like obeying the law).
jury: A group of citizens chosen by lot to help judges try the most serious crimes.
civic duty: Something a citizen should do for the life of the community, like voting or obeying the law.
democracy: A system in which power belongs to the people, who choose their leaders in free elections, and where freedoms are respected.
parliament: The assemblies that vote the laws. In France: the National Assembly and the Senate.
mayor: The person elected by the town council to run the town for 6 years.
class representative: A pupil elected by classmates to represent them and pass on their ideas.
children's town council: A group of children elected by other children to suggest and carry out projects for their town.
